name: Saccharomyces ferment

angle.text: Users of K-beauty essences, especially SK-II's Pitera, apply yeast ferment filtrate in pursuit of smoother, more radiant skin. Its fame comes largely from brand storytelling, and direct trials of the ingredient on appearance are almost absent.

summary: Yeast-fermentation filtrate used in essences like SK-II Pitera; the brand story is well known, direct trials are almost absent.
note: Evidence is largely brand-origin narrative; no ingredient-specific trials found.
currentQuick:
Saccharomyces ferment is the cosmetic name for a filtered yeast-fermentation product found in essences and serums. Its best-known form is Pitera in SK-II, which the brand says arose from observations of sake brewery workers.
Published human studies of the ingredient itself were not found; the only registered trial located covers probiotic skincare more generally.
How it works: Proponents describe the ferment as a mix of small molecules produced by yeast during fermentation, applied topically. No composition or mechanism is established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Used topically in cosmetics. SK-II products were involved in 2005-2006 complaints and temporary sales suspensions in China and South Korea, after which regulators reported trace elements were unlikely to harm health.
deepLead:
Saccharomyces ferment is a cosmetic ingredient name for the filtered product of yeast (Saccharomyces) fermentation, used in essences and serums. The best-known branded example is Pitera, the yeast-derived ingredient in the Japanese skincare line SK-II.
According to the brand history, SK-II was developed in Japan in the 1970s after scientists noticed that elderly sake brewery workers had smooth hands from handling fermenting yeast; the brand launched in the early 1980s. The Wikipedia article on the brand gives no composition for Pitera and cites no studies.
Published human research on this ingredient is very limited. A small registered trial examined a probiotic-containing skincare product range, which is a related but different category.

name: Kombucha ferment

angle.text: Kombucha ferment is used in serums and toners as an antioxidant, calming botanical aimed at fresher-looking skin. The evidence for skin appearance consists of lab-dish antioxidant data; human skin trials are untested.

summary: Tea or plant extract fermented with a kombucha culture; only lab-dish antioxidant data exist for skin.
note: No human skin trials found.
currentQuick:
Kombucha ferment is a cosmetic ingredient made by fermenting tea or botanical extracts with a kombucha culture. Marketing links it to antioxidant and soothing effects.
Published work consists of laboratory studies on cells and chemical assays; no human skincare trials were found.
How it works: The culture of bacteria and yeast converts sugars into organic acids and alters polyphenols in the extract; in vitro studies report higher antioxidant activity in some fermented extracts.
Risks and caveats: Topical safety data were not found. Reports of serious adverse events relate mainly to drinking home-brewed kombucha.
deepLead:
Kombucha ferment is a skincare ingredient name for products made by fermenting tea or plant extracts with a kombucha culture (a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast, often called SCOBY). Kombucha as a drink is a lightly sweetened fermented black tea, thought to have originated in China.
Laboratory work has fermented botanical extracts with kombucha cultures and measured antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, including a 2023 study of elderberry (Sambucus nigra) fruit ferment on human skin fibroblast cells. No human trials of kombucha ferment as a skincare ingredient were found.

name: Tremella mushroom

angle.text: Tremella, or snow fungus, is used in Asian skincare as a plant alternative to hyaluronic acid, promoted to hydrate skin and soften the look of fine lines. Support for that use comes from patents and brand claims rather than human trials.

summary: Snow fungus polysaccharide marketed as a hydrator; support is patents and reported claims, not trials.
note: No human skin trials found.
currentQuick:
Tremella is an edible gelatinous fungus whose polysaccharide extracts are used in Asian skincare as moisturisers and brightening agents.
The sources found are encyclopedic descriptions and patents; no clinical trials were found.
How it works: Its polysaccharides are described as water-absorbing and water-holding, and a patent reports inhibition of melanin formation.
Risks and caveats: No skincare safety data were found; the fungus is a long-established food.
deepLead:
Tremella fuciformis, known as snow fungus or silver ear, is an edible white gelatinous fungus cultivated commercially in China and used in Chinese cuisine and traditional medicine. Extracts, especially polysaccharides, appear in skincare products from China, Korea and Japan, where they are marketed as moisture-retaining and anti-wrinkle.
Patent literature describes a hot-water-extracted Tremella polysaccharide with water-holding capacity and melanin-inhibiting effects. No published clinical trials of topical Tremella were found.

name: Mugwort

angle.text: Mugwort extract is a staple of K-beauty toners and masks, used by people with reactive skin who want a calmer, less red complexion. Its folk use is long, while trials of its effect on skin appearance are absent.

summary: Artemisia herb used in K-beauty as a calming botanical; folk use is long, skin trials are absent and pollen allergy is common.
note: Pollen allergen; thujone content; avoided in pregnancy per herbal safety guidance.
currentQuick:
Mugwort refers to several Artemisia species used in food, folk medicine, moxibustion and, more recently, skincare billed as calming.
No human trials of mugwort skincare were found; evidence cited in sources is traditional use and preliminary lab findings.
How it works: Extracts contain terpenes such as cineole, camphor and thujone, which preliminary studies associate with antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity.
Risks and caveats: Mugwort pollen is a common allergen and the plant may trigger reactions in people sensitive to Asteraceae. Thujone is a neurotoxin at high concentrations, and herbal safety guidance advises against use in pregnancy.
deepLead:
Mugwort is a common name for several aromatic Artemisia species: Artemisia vulgaris in Europe, and A. argyi (Chinese mugwort) or A. princeps (Korean ssuk, Japanese yomogi) in East Asia. It has a long history in folk medicine, food, and moxibustion, and extracts are used in Korean skincare marketed as calming.
Mugwort pollen is a major cause of hay fever and allergic asthma, and the plant typically contains thujone, which at high concentrations has been linked to seizures and abortive effects. No published trials of mugwort skincare were found.

name: Houttuynia cordata

angle.text: Heartleaf extract appears in Korean toners, serums and sheet masks used for calming redness and oily, blemish-prone skin. Cell-culture data on inflammation exist, while human skin-appearance trials are essentially absent.

summary: Fish mint extract ("heartleaf") in K-beauty toners; cell data are encouraging, human skin trials are essentially absent.
note: Injected forms caused severe reactions; patch-test advice for topical use.
currentQuick:
Houttuynia cordata is a herb eaten in East and Southeast Asia and used in traditional medicine. Its extract, "heartleaf", is common in Korean skincare marketed for calming redness and oil.
Support comes mainly from cell studies and a small reported toner study; no controlled skin trials were found.
How it works: Flavonoids such as quercitrin are reported in cell studies to lower inflammatory mediators and offer antioxidant effects, with antibacterial activity against acne bacteria in vitro.
Risks and caveats: Contact dermatitis is reported in sensitive users. Injectable forms have caused severe allergic reactions, and high oral doses were toxic in animal studies.
deepLead:
Houttuynia cordata, called fish mint, heartleaf or chameleon plant, is a perennial native to Southeast Asia used as a vegetable and herb in Vietnam, Japan, Korea, northeastern India and southwestern China, and in traditional Chinese medicine. Its extract, marketed as "heartleaf", is a prominent ingredient in Korean skincare toners, serums and sheet masks.
Evidence on skin is mostly laboratory-based; Wikipedia notes there was no high-quality clinical research confirming safety or effectiveness as of 2018. Injectable preparations have caused severe allergic reactions.

name: Ginseng root extract

angle.text: Ginseng root extract is used in K-beauty and herbal skincare, promoted as an antioxidant that gives skin a healthier, more youthful look. Its topical effect on appearance has not been tested in trials.

summary: Korean-herb root extract sold as an antioxidant skincare ingredient, with no trials of its topical appearance effects.
note: Evidence comes from oral-use reviews and lab studies, not topical skin trials.
currentQuick:
Ginseng root extract comes from Panax ginseng, a root used in East Asian traditional medicine. In skincare it shows up in K-beauty and herbal products, marketed as antioxidant or soothing.
Research is mostly on oral ginseng for general health, where reviews found efficacy not established. No clinical trial of topical use for appearance was found.
How it works: Ginsenosides in the root reduced inflammatory and oxidative signalling in cell and animal studies; these were not skin-appearance experiments.
Risks and caveats: Oral ginseng has reported side effects (headache, insomnia, raised blood pressure) and drug interactions such as with warfarin. Topical products carry standard external-use and irritation warnings.
deepLead:
Ginseng root extract is a preparation made from the root of Panax ginseng, a perennial herb native to mountainous parts of Korea, northeast China and the Russian Far East that has long been used in East Asian folk medicine. In skincare it is used as an ingredient in K-beauty and herbal products, where it is marketed mainly as an antioxidant or soothing botanical; one US-listed topical product containing it is a herbal medicated soap.
Most of the published research concerns oral ginseng for general health claims rather than topical use for appearance. Systematic reviews of randomised trials concluded that the efficacy of ginseng root extract could not be established beyond doubt for any indication studied, and laboratory studies have reported anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in cells and animals. No clinical trial of topical ginseng root extract for skin appearance appears among the sources reviewed.

name: Portulaca oleracea

angle.text: Purslane extract appears in soothing essences and moisturisers, where users reach for it to calm irritated skin and improve its look. Support consists of lab and animal data; skin-appearance trials in people are untested.

summary: Edible succulent weed used as a soothing skincare botanical, backed by lab and animal data but no skin-appearance trials.
note: Evidence is from lab and animal studies; no topical human appearance trials found.
currentQuick:
Purslane is a common edible succulent used in folk medicine, now added to K-beauty-style soothing products.
Research reports anti-inflammatory and wound-healing effects in cells and animals. No clinical trials of topical use for appearance were found.
How it works: Flavonoids, alkaloids and fatty acids in the plant show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in laboratory assays.
Risks and caveats: Leaves are high in oxalates when eaten. Topical product labels advise avoiding broken skin and stopping use if irritation occurs.
deepLead:
Portulaca oleracea, commonly purslane, is a warm-climate succulent annual eaten as a leafy vegetable in the Mediterranean, Middle East, Asia and Mexico and used in folk medicine in many countries. In skincare, extracts appear in soothing and moisturising products; one DailyMed-listed essence combines Portulaca oleracea extract with niacinamide, glycerin and lotus flower extract.
Laboratory research describes anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and wound-healing activity. A 2015 review catalogued its flavonoids, alkaloids and fatty acids and their reported pharmacological effects, and a mouse study reported faster excision-wound closure with a crude topical preparation. No controlled clinical trial of topical purslane for skin appearance was found.

name: Scutellaria baicalensis root extract

angle.text: Baikal skullcap root extract is used in cosmetics as an anti-inflammatory or brightening botanical, aimed at redness and uneven tone. Small human trials are registered, but little has been published on its effect on skin appearance.

summary: Chinese skullcap root extract used as an anti-inflammatory or brightening ingredient, with small trials registered but little published human evidence.
note: Contact allergy reported; oral products linked to liver injury case reports.
currentQuick:
A root extract from Baikal skullcap, a staple of traditional Chinese medicine, now used in some skincare for anti-inflammatory or brightening claims.
Evidence is mostly lab studies; two small hyperpigmentation cream trials are registered.
How it works: Flavonoids such as baicalin and wogonin showed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in cell and animal studies.
Risks and caveats: A case report describes contact allergy to a cosmetic containing it, and oral supplements have been linked to liver injury in case reports.
deepLead:
Scutellaria baicalensis root extract comes from Baikal skullcap, a mint-family plant whose dried root (huangqin) is one of the 50 fundamental herbs of traditional Chinese medicine. Its main flavonoids include baicalin, baicalein and wogonin. In cosmetics it is used as an anti-inflammatory or brightening botanical.
Laboratory studies report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, and a 2025 safety assessment reviewed its use as a cosmetic ingredient. A case report documents allergic contact dermatitis to a cosmetic containing it. Two small registered trials have tested creams for hyperpigmentation, though results were not located.

name: Perilla seed extract

angle.text: Perilla seed extract is included in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 and antioxidant ingredient, promoted for softer, healthier-looking skin. Human studies of its appearance effects have not been done.

summary: Seed extract from an Asian culinary herb, used as a plant omega-3 skincare ingredient with no human appearance studies.
note: Seed allergy and contact dermatitis are documented.
currentQuick:
Perilla seed extract comes from a plant used in Korean and other Asian cooking, and is sold in some skincare as a botanical.
Research is limited to lab and animal studies; no human appearance trials were found.
How it works: The extract and its component luteolin reduced inflammatory signalling in animal and cell studies.
Risks and caveats: Perilla seed allergy, including anaphylaxis, is documented in children and adults, and contact dermatitis can occur.
deepLead:
Perilla seed extract is derived from the seeds of Perilla frutescens, a mint-family annual used in Korean, Chinese, Japanese and Indian cooking; the seeds contain roughly 38 to 45 percent oil. It appears in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 or antioxidant ingredient.
Published work consists mainly of laboratory and animal studies, including anti-inflammatory effects in mouse colitis models and an in vitro hair-loss study. Perilla seed allergy is documented in children, and handling can cause contact dermatitis. No clinical study of perilla seed extract for skin appearance was found.

name: Camellia japonica extract

angle.text: Japanese camellia extract is used in some cosmetics, with Korean patent filings describing it for anti-ageing, whitening and anti-inflammatory purposes. Evidence for that use is limited to a mouse study; human data are untested.

summary: Japanese camellia botanical used in some cosmetics, with one mouse study and no human data.
note: Only animal and patent material found.
currentQuick:
An extract from the Japanese camellia shrub, used in some cosmetics.
The only published research found is a 2025 mouse study; no human studies exist in the sources reviewed.
How it works: In mice, topical extract reduced skin inflammation markers in an atopic dermatitis model.
Risks and caveats: No safety data for human cosmetic use were found.
deepLead:
Camellia japonica extract is derived from the Japanese camellia, a flowering evergreen tree or shrub; its leaves can be made into tea and are reported to contain anti-inflammatory terpenoids such as lupeol and squalene. It is used in some cosmetics as a botanical ingredient, and Korean patent filings from 2004 and 2005 describe cosmetic compositions using it for anti-ageing, whitening and anti-inflammatory purposes.
Evidence is thin: a 2025 study in hairless mice reported that topical extract reduced atopic-dermatitis-like signs. No human studies were found.

name: Hemp seed oil

angle.text: Hemp seed oil is used in moisturisers and body care by people wanting soft, well-hydrated skin, and is often chosen for its high linoleic acid content. Skin-specific trials are few, so its appearance benefits rest mostly on general emollient reasoning.

summary: A fatty-acid-rich plant oil used in moisturisers and body care; the skin-specific evidence is thin.
note: Not the same as CBD extract; no published trials of skin or hair benefit were found.
currentQuick:
Hemp seed oil is pressed from the seeds of low-THC hemp plants and is high in linoleic and alpha-linolenic fatty acids. It appears in moisturisers, soaps and haircare products.
Most of the published work describes its chemistry and quality. Registered human studies of topical use exist but no results were found.
How it works: Proponents attribute benefits to its essential fatty acids, which are described as moisturising and nourishing. This has been described mainly in product labelling and composition studies rather than skin trials.
Risks and caveats: Topical products carry standard 'external use only' labelling. Analytical studies have measured trace cannabinoids in some commercial oils. No clinical trial data on skin outcomes were identified.
deepLead:
Hemp seed oil is a plant oil pressed from the seeds of low-THC varieties of Cannabis sativa. It is used as a food oil, in body-care products such as soaps, shampoos and moisturisers, and in industrial products such as paints and finishes. It is rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids, chiefly linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid.
In skincare and haircare, it is marketed as a moisturising, nourishing ingredient. The sources available for this article are mostly chemical and food-science analyses of the oil rather than trials of its effect on skin or hair; two small registered human studies of topical hemp oil products are listed, and neither has published results in the material reviewed.
Hemp seed oil is distinct from cannabidiol (CBD) extracts made from the flower and leaf. Seeds contain no cannabinoids themselves, but trace amounts can be carried onto the oil from plant material during processing, which is why analytical studies have measured cannabinoid content in commercial oils.

name: Volcanic ash

angle.text: Volcanic ash appears in some K-beauty masks and cleansers, promoted to absorb oil and leave oily skin looking matte. The sources found describe the geology of ash, and trials of any skin benefit are untested.

summary: A sebum-absorbing mineral in some K-beauty masks; the sources found describe the geology, not any skin benefit.
note: No cosmetic-use studies found; raw eruption ash is an irritant.
currentQuick:
Volcanic ash is fine volcanic rock and glass. Ground volcanic materials appear in some skincare masks and cleansers as oil-absorbing ingredients.
The literature found covers volcanology and exposure hazards, not cosmetic effects.
How it works: Users and marketing describe it as absorbing sebum; no study of this on human skin was identified.
Risks and caveats: Eruption ash is abrasive and can irritate eyes, skin and airways. Cosmetic safety data were not found.
deepLead:
Volcanic ash is fine fragmented rock, mineral crystal and volcanic glass, under 2 mm in diameter, produced by explosive eruptions. Its chemistry varies with the magma type, from silica-poor basaltic to silica-rich rhyolitic ash.
In skincare, ground volcanic ash, volcanic clay and related volcanic minerals are used in some products, particularly Korean-origin masks and cleansers, as sebum-absorbing ingredients. The sources reviewed for this article describe the material in geological and health-hazard terms and do not document cosmetic use; no study of cosmetic volcanic ash on human skin was identified.

name: Witch hazel extract

angle.text: Witch hazel is a classic astringent toner used by people with oily or blemish-prone skin to reduce shine and give a tighter feel. Lab data on its properties exist, while human skin trials are lacking.

summary: The classic astringent toner botanical; lab data exist, human skin trials do not.
note: Toner distillates typically contain alcohol; no human skincare trials found.
currentQuick:
Witch hazel extract comes from the bark and leaves of a North American shrub and is traditionally used as an astringent toner. Native American and later settler use on swellings and inflammations is part of its history.
The published literature found is laboratory work, with no human trials of its cosmetic effect.
How it works: It is rich in tannins such as hamamelitannin. Laboratory studies report antibacterial effects of a standardised extract; how this relates to skin toning has not been tested in trials.
Risks and caveats: Safety data were not reviewed in the available sources. Traditional toner distillates are made with alcohol.
deepLead:
Witch hazel extract is a preparation made from the bark and leaves of Hamamelis virginiana, a shrub native to eastern North America. It is best known as the astringent 'witch hazel' sold as a skin toner, a product made by distilling the plant material in dilute alcohol.
Native American peoples used preparations of the bark and leaves for swellings and external inflammations, and the remedy was adopted by early settlers in New England. The plant contains tannins, including a type called hamamelitannin.
The sources reviewed contain laboratory studies of witch hazel extract, mainly antibacterial and chemical analyses, but no published human trial of its use as a skincare toner was identified.

name: Pine bark extract

angle.text: Maritime pine bark extract (Pycnogenol) is taken or applied as an antioxidant in anti-aging and skin-brightening routines. It has been studied for many conditions, but its appearance effects are not the main focus of that research.

summary: A polyphenol antioxidant supplement (Pycnogenol); studied for many conditions, not for appearance.
note: A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the conditions studied; no appearance trials found.
currentQuick:
Pine bark extract is a proanthocyanidin-rich supplement from French maritime pine, best known under the trademark Pycnogenol. It is promoted as an antioxidant.
Human trials have looked at blood pressure, ADHD and other conditions; a Cochrane review judged the evidence insufficient. No skin-appearance trials were found.
How it works: Laboratory work reports antioxidant activity and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases, which are linked to collagen breakdown.
Risks and caveats: Safety information was not detailed in the reviewed sources.
deepLead:
Maritime pine bark extract is a dietary supplement made from the bark of Pinus pinaster, consisting mostly of proanthocyanidins (procyanidins). Pycnogenol is a trademarked standardised version containing 70% procyanidins. It is sold as an antioxidant and is included in some supplement and skincare products.
According to Wikipedia, the French researcher Jack Masquelier developed the extract after reading an account of Jacques Cartier's expedition in which Native Americans were described drinking a bark tea, and he used the name Pycnogenol in 1979.
Researchers have studied the extract in conditions including asthma, ADHD, blood pressure, venous insufficiency and osteoarthritis. A Cochrane review, updated in 2020, found insufficient evidence for efficacy across these conditions. No trial of its effect on facial appearance was identified in the reviewed sources.

name: Mistletoe extract

angle.text: Mistletoe extract appears as a botanical in some Korean-style skincare products, where it is promoted for soothing and general skin health. Its research is in complementary cancer care rather than skin, so the appearance link is untested.

summary: A mistletoe botanical used in some skincare; its research is in cancer care, not skin.
note: Plant toxins (viscumin) are documented; no skin trials found.
currentQuick:
Mistletoe extract comes from Viscum album. Injectable extracts such as Iscador have been used as complementary cancer treatments, and the plant appears as a botanical in some skincare.
Human trials examine cancer patients; none examine skin or appearance.
How it works: Mistletoe lectins have been reported in laboratory and patient studies to stimulate immune signalling such as TNF-alpha and interleukins.
Risks and caveats: The plant contains the toxin viscumin, which Wikipedia says works like ricin. Topical cosmetic safety was not covered in the reviewed sources.
deepLead:
Mistletoe extract is prepared from European mistletoe (Viscum album), a semi-parasitic plant. Standardised or proprietary extracts such as Iscador have been used as complementary cancer treatments, mainly in German-speaking countries, and the plant also appears as a botanical in some Korean-style skincare products.
The plant's toxins include viscumin, which inhibits ribosomal protein synthesis by a mechanism similar to ricin's; European mistletoe is described as more toxic than American mistletoe. Medicinal extracts contain mistletoe lectins that have been studied for immune-stimulating effects.
Published human research concerns cancer patients, not skin. No study of mistletoe extract on skin or appearance was identified in the sources reviewed.

name: Noni fruit extract

angle.text: Noni extract is sold as juice, supplements and cosmetics, promoted as an antioxidant for a brighter, more youthful complexion. Evidence for skin appearance is lab-only.

summary: A Pacific fruit extract sold as an antioxidant; skin evidence is lab-only and liver-safety concerns are documented for oral products.
note: A 2024 review links oral noni products to liver disease risk; FDA 2018 warning letter on claims.
currentQuick:
Noni is a tropical fruit used traditionally in the Pacific and now sold as juice, supplements and in cosmetics as an antioxidant botanical.
Wikipedia reports no confirmed clinical efficacy for any use. Skin research is limited to cell studies.
How it works: An anthraquinone from the fruit was reported to boost extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured fibroblasts; this has not been tested in people.
Risks and caveats: Anthraquinones can be harmful, and a 2024 review is cited as linking oral noni products to liver disease. The FDA issued a 2018 warning letter over drug claims.
deepLead:
Noni fruit extract comes from Morinda citrifolia, a tropical shrub of the coffee family spread across the Pacific by Polynesian sailors. The pungent fruit was historically a famine food, and parts of the plant were used in Polynesian medicine as a tonic. Today it is sold as juice, powders, supplements and in cosmetics.
The fruit contains anthraquinones, iridoids, flavonoids, scopoletin and other compounds. Wikipedia states there is no confirmed evidence of clinical efficacy for any intended use, and a 2024 review is cited there linking noni products to liver disease risk. In 2018 the US FDA issued a warning letter to a noni marketer for unapproved drug claims.
Laboratory work has reported that an anthraquinone from noni induced extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured human skin fibroblasts, but no trial of noni on skin appearance was identified.

name: Moringa

angle.text: Moringa seed oil and leaf extract are used in skin and hair products as a light moisturiser and antioxidant for smoother, healthier-looking skin. Antioxidant lab data exist, while skin-appearance trials are untested.

summary: A tropical tree whose seed oil and leaf extract show up in skin products, with antioxidant lab data but no skin-appearance trials.
note: Evidence is lab-based; oral safety data are limited.
currentQuick:
Moringa is a tree grown across the tropics. In skin care its seed oil and leaf extracts appear in moisturisers and body oils, marketed for moisturising and antioxidant effects.
Laboratory studies show leaf extracts have antioxidant activity, but no human trial found tests it for skin appearance.
How it works: Proposed benefits rest on its fatty-acid-rich oil acting as an emollient and on phenolic compounds such as quercetin and kaempferol that show antioxidant activity in the lab.
Risks and caveats: Topical products are generally labelled for external use. Oral use has limited human toxicity data and possible drug-metabolism interactions per Wikipedia, and Australia and New Zealand declined novel-food approval in 2025.
deepLead:
Moringa usually refers to Moringa oleifera, a fast-growing tree native to northern India and widely cultivated across the tropics, also known as the drumstick or horseradish tree. Its leaves, pods and seeds are eaten, and its seed oil (sometimes called ben oil) is used as a base in skin- and hair-care products.
In cosmetics, moringa appears as a seed oil or leaf extract in creams, body oils and similar products, typically marketed for moisturising or antioxidant benefits. Laboratory studies have measured antioxidant activity in leaf extracts. Published review literature describes the plant mainly in terms of nutrition and general medicinal use rather than controlled evidence for facial appearance.
Wikipedia states that despite considerable preliminary research, no high-quality evidence has been found that moringa affects health or disease. No clinical trial found in the registries searched tests moringa for skin appearance.

name: Yuzu extract

angle.text: Yuzu extract is used in Asian skincare as a vitamin C botanical, promoted for brightening and evening out skin tone. Lab antioxidant and pigment data exist, and skin trials are untested.

summary: A citrus extract sold as a vitamin C botanical in Asian skin care, with lab antioxidant and pigment data but no skin trials.
note: Evidence is limited to cell and animal studies.
currentQuick:
Yuzu extract comes from a Japanese and Korean citrus fruit and is used in some skin-care products for its vitamin C and polyphenol content.
Research is limited to laboratory and animal studies; no human skin trial was found.
How it works: In cell studies a yuzu seed compound, nomilin, showed antioxidant activity and lowered melanin production in cultured melanoma cells.
Risks and caveats: No specific safety data for cosmetic use were found; citrus ingredients can irritate or sensitise some skin generally.
deepLead:
Yuzu (Citrus junos) is a tart, aromatic citrus fruit believed to have originated in central China and now grown mainly in Japan and Korea. Extracts of the peel, juice or seed appear in some Asian skin-care products, usually marketed for their vitamin C and polyphenol content.
Published work on yuzu extract consists mostly of laboratory and animal studies on antioxidant, antiplatelet and pigment-related activity. No human trial of yuzu extract for skin appearance was found.

name: Horse oil

angle.text: Horse oil (ma-yu) is used in Japanese and Korean creams as a rich emollient, chosen because its fatty acids resemble human skin lipids. Support comes from small formulation and cell studies, with human appearance trials untested.

summary: An animal-derived emollient oil from Japanese and Korean skin care, backed by small formulation and cell studies only.
note: Studies are small and mostly by developers; no independent human trials found.
currentQuick:
Horse oil is a fat from horses used as an emollient in some Japanese and Korean skin-care products. Makers point to its fatty acids resembling those in human skin.
Research is limited to small formulation, cell and patch studies; no independent clinical trial was found.
How it works: It acts as an emollient supplying unsaturated fatty acids; lab work reports barrier-supporting and antioxidant effects in cultured keratinocytes.
Risks and caveats: No safety data specific to people were found in the sources reviewed. It is an animal-derived product, and researchers have studied methods for detecting adulterated oil.
deepLead:
Horse oil (ma-yu in Japanese and Korean cosmetic usage) is a fat rendered from horse tissue, used as an emollient ingredient in skin-care products, particularly in East Asia. Its fatty-acid profile, including linoleic and palmitoleic acids, has been described as similar to that of human skin lipids.
Evidence consists of small formulation and laboratory studies, including work from Korean research groups on microneedle patches and on cultured skin cells. No independent clinical trial in people was found.

name: Starfish extract

angle.text: Starfish extract is a K-beauty marine ingredient promoted for moisturising and regenerating skin, inspired by starfish regrowing lost arms. Support is limited to a zebrafish study and patents; human effects are untested.

summary: A K-beauty marine ingredient inspired by starfish regeneration, supported only by a zebrafish study and patents.
note: No human skin studies found.
currentQuick:
Starfish extract appears in some Korean skin-care products as a moisturising or regenerating ingredient, drawing on starfish's ability to regrow limbs.
Only cell and zebrafish research and patents exist; no human trial was found.
How it works: In one study, fractions from regenerating starfish tissue boosted cell proliferation and migration in wound-healing assays.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data were found. Wikipedia notes that some starfish contain saponins and, in certain species, toxins, though cosmetic extracts were not addressed.
deepLead:
Starfish extract is a preparation from the tissues of sea stars, listed in some Korean beauty products as a moisturising or regenerating ingredient. Starfish are known for regrowing lost arms, and some researchers study their tissues for regenerative bioactive molecules.
Published evidence is very limited: a 2016 zebrafish study and a few patents. No human trial of starfish extract on skin was found.
